The catch, proven repeatedly in the last sweep, is that most Italian postings require native or fluent Italian — so **the language requirement is the first thing to check on every posting, and "not stated" is not the same as "English is fine"**. Companies and channels to work: Italian tech and scale-ups (indigo.ai, Satispay, Scalapay, Bending Spoons, Casavo, Translated, iGenius, Vedrai, Aidexa, Soldo, Moneyfarm, Young Platform, Musixmatch, Prima, Cortilia, Fatture in Cloud, Qomodo, Docsity) and Iberian/Southern-European remote-friendly employers (Factorial, Typeform, Jobandtalent, Cabify, Glovo, Unbabel, Sword Health, Feedzai, Talkdesk, OutSystems, Remote.com). Also work `euremotejobs.com` country paths for Italy, Spain and Portugal, and `join.com` / `jobs.personio.com` / `jobs.smartrecruiters.com` searches scoped to Italy and Iberia.

Any of his four tracks is fine; employment or contract.

Note that join.com and Personio search results run weeks stale — low join.com IDs are reliably dead, so prefer the freshest listings and verify each one.

Save to `/home/claude/sweep-2026-08-05/rows-I.json`:

1	---
2	name: job-hunt
3	description: >-
4	  Find, verify and rank live job and contract openings that fit Prabhavit's CV — AI/automation
5	  engineering, forward-deployed and solutions engineering, full-stack product engineering,
6	  technical PM — remote-first from Italy but worldwide in scope, delivered as a ranked .xlsx
7	  shortlist. Use this skill whenever the conversation turns to looking for work — "find me some
8	  jobs", "any new roles this week", "who's hiring for X", "check openings at a named company", "any
9	  freelance or contract gigs going", "is this posting worth applying to" — or when asked to
10	  compare or re-rank roles already found. Trigger even when the request is vague ("anything
11	  interesting out there?"), names no job board, or mentions only a company or a technology
12	  rather than a role.
13	---
14	
15	# Job hunt
16	
17	Prabhavit is looking for work right now — his FlowSpace contract ended in July 2026. What
18	helps him is a short list of openings that are **real, currently open, and genuinely open to
19	him**, each with an honest reason it's worth an application. What hurts him is volume: a dead
20	link, a role that turns out to be US-payroll-only, or a staff-level posting he has no chance at
21	costs him more time than a missed opportunity does. Bias the whole process towards precision.
22	
23	Two references do the heavy lifting:
24	
25	- `references/candidate-profile.md` — what "good fit" means. **Read it before every sweep.** It holds his eligibility, target titles, seniority band, hard gates and preferences.
26	- `references/sources.md` — the tested search playbook: which domains and URL patterns actually return live postings, which are dead ends, and the specific ways postings lie. **Read it before your first search in a session.**
27	
28	Don't interview him before starting. He's already told the skill what he wants; ask at most one
29	question, and only when the answer would change the entire sweep (for example, if he names a
30	company that has no public board). Otherwise run the default sweep and note your assumptions in
31	the reply.
32	
33	## Step 1 — frame the sweep
34	
35	Set five parameters before searching. Anything the request specifies overrides these defaults:
36	
37	| Parameter | Default |
38	|---|---|
39	| Tracks | All four from the profile, weighted A (AI/automation) > B (forward-deployed/solutions) > C (full-stack/product) > D (technical PM) |
40	| Geography | Worldwide, prioritised by the eligibility tiers in the profile — mostly Tier 1, a minority of Tier 3 |
41	| Work basis | Employment **and** contract/freelance, in the same sheet, flagged so he can compare a day rate against a salary |
42	| Freshness | Posted within 30 days; prefer the last 7 |
43	| Size | 12–20 verified roles. Expect roughly **one in three candidates to survive verification** — dead postings, board-index degradation, false "Remote" labels — so plan on fetching 3–4× the target. If the first pass lands short, run a second discovery pass with different vocabulary rather than shipping four rows. |
44	
45	A narrow request ("just contract work", "only n8n stuff", "anything at ElevenLabs") narrows the
46	sweep — don't pad it back out with unrelated roles to hit a count.
47	
48	## Step 2 — sweep wide before filtering
49	
50	Cast a much wider net than the final sheet, because most candidates die at verification. Aim for
51	**50+ raw candidates**; fewer than ~30 means the sweep was too narrow, and the fix is almost
52	always vocabulary — the same job is posted as "AI Automation Engineer", "Applied AI Engineer",
53	"Solutions Engineer" and "Automation Consultant" at four different companies.
54	
55	Verification is what caps the size of the sheet, so spend the discovery budget in ways that make
56	verification cheap. **Board APIs verify a whole company in one call** (§5 of `sources.md`), so
57	when several candidates come from the same org, check the org once instead of fetching each
58	posting. Where subagents are available, give each one a source family *and* have it return
59	already-verified rows — parallel verification is what turns a 6-row sheet into a 15-row one.
60	
61	Run these in parallel in a single message (see `sources.md` for exact syntax and templates):
62	
63	1. Two or three `WebSearch` calls with `allowed_domains` on the ATS hosts — one per track.
64	2. One contract-vocabulary query using the literal words that work: `"contract"`, `"6-month contract"`, `freelance`, `B2B`, `part time`, `fractional`.
65	3. One stack-keyword query — `n8n`, `low-code`, `AI agents`, `Bubble.io`. These postings are much less crowded and are his sharpest edge.
66	4. Two or three board fetches — euremotejobs region paths, remoterocketship with `sort=DateAdded`, himalayas (serialize these, it rate-limits).
67	
68	If subagents are available, fan the sweep out: give each agent one source family and a fixed
69	return shape (title, company, url, location wording, comp, posted date, basis). Verification is
70	fetch-heavy, so parallelising the discovery leaves budget for it. Tell each agent to use only
71	WebSearch/WebFetch — curl and python fetching are prohibited in this environment.
72	
73	## Step 3 — filter against the profile
74	
75	Apply the hard gates from `candidate-profile.md` — language requirements he can't meet, deep ML
76	specialisation, agencies and aggregator reposts with no named end client, unpaid or
77	talent-pool listings. Being outside the EU is **not** a gate any more; it moves a role to
78	eligibility Tier 3 with a `Relocation` or `Sponsorship` flag.
79	
80	Keep a short list of notable drops and why. When the sheet comes back with 14 roles instead of
81	40, he should be able to see that the filter did the work rather than wondering whether the
82	search was lazy.
83	
84	## Step 4 — verify every survivor by fetching it
85	
86	He will click every link in the sheet, so every row must come from a page you actually loaded.
87	Never list a role from a search snippet alone, and never reconstruct a URL that looks plausible.
88	
89	For each candidate:
90	
91	- Normalise the URL first (strip Ashby's `?embed=js`, `/application`, `?utm_data=…`; add `?language=en` on Personio).
92	- Fetch it, and pull: exact title, company, the **eligibility sentence** (not the word "Remote" in the title), comp or rate if disclosed, posted date, seniority requirement, and whether it's employment or contract.
93	- **If a single-posting fetch comes back describing many different jobs, the posting is closed** — Greenhouse silently serves the board index for dead roles and nothing else signals it. Drop it.
94	- Drop anything you can't confirm is live. A quiet omission is better than a broken row.
95	- When a posting looks strong but the fetch is ambiguous, check the company's JSON board API (`sources.md` §5) rather than guessing.
96	
97	## Step 5 — score honestly
98	
99	```
100	Fit = role & track match        30
101	    + eligibility & work basis  25
102	    + stack overlap             20
103	    + seniority realism         15
104	    + signal quality            10
105	```
106	
107	- **Role & track match** — how close the actual responsibilities are to what he's done, not how good the title sounds.
108	- **Eligibility & work basis** — Tier 1 (workable from Italy today) scores full marks; Tier 2 (non-EU Europe, remote) most of them; Tier 3 (relocation or sponsorship) a fraction. A company willing to engage a contractor abroad scores as Tier 1 even if it's US-based.
109	- **Stack overlap** — named tools he has shipped with beat adjacent ones. `n8n` in a JD is worth more than a generic "Python required".
110	- **Seniority realism** — will they actually interview someone with ~3 years and no CS degree?
111	- **Signal quality** — freshness, disclosed comp, company type, clear scope.
112	
113	Use the range. If every role scores 82–88 the scores carry no information and he can't triage;
114	a real sweep produces a spread. Bands: **80+** apply this week · **65–79** solid, worth an
115	application · **50–64** worth a look if the top of the list dries up. Below 50, leave it out and
116	say why in chat if it was interesting.
117	
118	## Step 6 — build the spreadsheet
119	
120	Write the roles to JSON and run the bundled script — it owns the column layout, tier colours,
121	fit colour-scale, filters and the "Search notes" sheet, so week-to-week shortlists stay
122	comparable and no run has to reinvent openpyxl:
123	
124	```bash
125	python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/build_shortlist.py --in roles.json --out "Role shortlist — 5 Aug 2026.xlsx"
126	```
127	
128	Use the absolute path to the skill directory — the working directory during a sweep is rarely
129	the skill folder.
130	
131	The JSON shape is documented in the script's docstring. Fill `sweep_notes` — sources swept,
132	queries run, raw/gated/verified counts, notable drops — because that sheet is how he judges
133	whether the search covered the ground. Then deliver the file with `SendUserFile`.
134	
135	## Step 7 — report briefly in chat
136	
137	Short and useful; the spreadsheet holds the detail. Roughly:
138	
139	- One line on what was swept and what came back (`19 verified from ~60 candidates`).
140	- The top three, one line each: role, company, and the specific reason it fits.
141	- What to do first — which one or two to apply to today, and why those.
142	- **A market read** — the part a bare list can't give him. What the roles you saw are paying (bands, or rates for contract work), which title framings are getting posted and which have dried up, and anything about his own profile that is visibly costing him applications. The most useful example so far: the Bubble.io/no-code weighting on his CV reads as "no-code contractor" to code-first teams, which is a fixable presentation problem rather than a skills gap. Say that kind of thing plainly — a shortlist plus one true observation beats a longer shortlist.
143	- Where a role would be a contract engagement with a non-EU company, note anything he'd need to handle on his side (invoicing as a Partita IVA, W-8BEN for US clients, Deel/Wise rails) — briefly, and only when it's actually load-bearing for that role.
144	
145	Don't re-tabulate the sheet in chat, and don't pad with encouragement.
146	
147	## Judgment calls
148	
149	- **"Is this posting any good for me?"** with a single link — skip the sweep entirely. Fetch it, score it against the profile, answer in chat with the honest verdict and what to emphasise if he applies. No spreadsheet unless he asks.
150	- **A named company** — fetch its board directly (`job-boards.greenhouse.io/<company>`, or an `allowed_domains` search on the company name) instead of running a generic sweep.
151	- **A repeat run** — if an earlier shortlist exists in this session or in the project, dedupe against it and mark what's new, so he isn't re-reading last week's list. Say how many were carried over.
152	- **A thin sweep** — if verification leaves only a handful, deliver the handful and say plainly what you'd change next time (different vocabulary, wider geography, contract-only pass). Don't inflate the sheet.
153	- **He corrects a preference** — a rate expectation, a company he'd never join, a city he would move to — write it into `references/candidate-profile.md` so the next run inherits it.
154	- **Something in the sweep is worth acting on beyond applying** (a company hiring three roles he fits, a recruiter contact in the posting) — mention it in the chat reply; it's often more valuable than one more row.
155	
156	## Files in this skill
157	
158	```
159	job-hunt/
160	├── SKILL.md
161	├── references/
162	│   ├── candidate-profile.md   — what "good fit" means; keep it current
163	│   └── sources.md             — tested search playbook, dead ends, verification traps
164	└── scripts/

91	1. **Requires professional fluency in a language he doesn't speak** — most often Italian (beginner), German, French, Dutch, Spanish. English-only requirements are fine.
92	2. **Deep specialist requirements he cannot evidence**: ML research / publications / PhD, training or fine-tuning foundation models from scratch, CUDA/GPU kernel work, distributed-systems SRE at scale, mobile-native (Swift/Kotlin), heavy data engineering (Spark/dbt/Airflow).
93	3. **Staffing agency, body shop, or aggregator repost with no named end client**, and outsourcing firms advertising "remote Europe" that are really India/LATAM delivery centres (common on Lever — verify the entity before trusting it).
94	4. **Unpaid, equity-only, commission-only, or a talent-pool listing** with no actual open engagement.
95	5. **Closed, expired, or unverifiable posting** — see the verification step in SKILL.md.
96	
97	Note what is *not* a hard gate any more: being outside the EU, needing sponsorship, or
98	requiring relocation. Those become Tier 3 with a flag. A US-only or APAC-only role that
99	cannot engage a contractor abroad and won't relocate him is still a drop — but say so
100	because the posting rules him out, not because of where the company sits.
101	
102	## Preferences (score adjustments, not gates)
103	
104	Better fit:
105	- Fully remote with an explicit Europe/EMEA/worldwide eligibility statement.
106	- Startups and scale-ups (roughly 10–300 people) where one person owns a problem end to end.
107	- Companies whose product *is* AI/automation/agents, or whose operations are automation-heavy.
108	- Postings that value shipping and portfolio over credentials — "CS degree required" converts poorly for him even where he could do the work.
109	- Contract engagements with a defined scope and a stated rate.
110	- Salary or rate disclosed. Disclosure is a mild positive signal on top of the number itself.
111	- Posted within the last 30 days; within 7 days is materially better.
112	
113	Worse fit:
114	- Big-corporate, heavy-process environments and long enterprise hiring loops.
115	- Timezone requirements demanding full US working-hours coverage — workable for a contract, wearing for a permanent role, so flag it rather than dropping it.
116	- Roles that are pure maintenance of a legacy stack with no AI/automation surface.
117	
118	**Salary / rate expectation:** not yet stated. Ask once, in passing, the first time it
119	matters, and record the answer here. Until then report what postings disclose and don't
120	guess at what's acceptable.
121	
122	**Work basis (stated 2026-08-05):** he is **open to contractor roles as well as employment**
123	— neither is a fallback, so carry both in every sweep and let fit decide the ranking. A
124	US-based company that engages international contractors counts as **Tier 1, not Tier 3**;
125	only US-payroll-only postings drop out. He also asked for roles **outside the EU** to be
126	included, which is why geography is worldwide with tiering rather than an EU filter.

1	# Search playbook — where the roles actually are
2	
3	Everything here was tested with the WebSearch / WebFetch tools rather than assumed. The point
4	of writing it down is that a job sweep burns most of its budget on dead ends: SPA boards that
5	render nothing, aggregators reposting stale listings, and postings that quietly closed weeks
6	ago. Use the verified paths, skip the graveyard, and spend the saved calls on verification.
7	
8	**Never fetch job pages with curl, wget, or python requests.** WebSearch and WebFetch are the
9	only permitted ways to reach the web here. If something is blocked, it stays blocked.
10	
11	---
12	
13	## 1. The two mechanisms
14	
15	**WebSearch with `allowed_domains`** — this is a *hard* filter, unlike a `site:` operator which
16	is only a ranking hint. Restricting to ATS hosts is the single highest-precision move
17	available: it returns individual live postings instead of SEO farms and aggregators. Prefer it.
18	
19	```
20	WebSearch(query="AI automation engineer remote Europe",
21	          allowed_domains=["jobs.ashbyhq.com","job-boards.greenhouse.io"])
22	```
23	
24	**WebFetch on a board listing page** — good boards expose path-based taxonomies (region,
25	country, category) that return dozens of listings in one call, with posting ages. Use these
26	for breadth and for freshness, then verify individual postings.
27	
28	Run several of both in parallel in one message. Sweeping six sources at once and then
29	verifying is far faster than a serial crawl — with one exception noted below (Himalayas).
30	
31	---
32	
33	## 2. ATS domains, ranked by yield
34	
35	| Domain | Why | Notes |
36	|---|---|---|
37	| `jobs.ashbyhq.com` | **Best single source for discovery.** Modern AI companies, EMEA-aware titles, no index-page noise. The only ATS that reliably discloses **salary bands**, often in several currencies. | Canonical URL is `jobs.ashbyhq.com/<org>/<uuid>` — strip `?embed=js`, `/application`, `?utm_data=…`, `?locationId=…`. **But read the posting through the API, not the page:** Ashby HTML pages frequently come back as an unrendered JS shell ("You need to enable JavaScript"), and a shell looks exactly like a closed role. One API call per org covers every posting it has, so it's cheaper anyway. |
38	| `job-boards.greenhouse.io` | High volume, clean single postings. Salary usually absent. | Note the **hyphenated** host. |
39	| `job-boards.eu.greenhouse.io` | EU data-residency variant that surfaces European employers the `.com` host misses (JetBrains, Prolific, Clarity AI, saasgroup). | Query it *in addition to* the `.com` host, not instead. |
40	| `jobs.smartrecruiters.com` | Solid individual postings, location often in the title string. | Use this host. **`careers.smartrecruiters.com` returns only board index pages — skip it.** |
41	| `join.com` | Good for European startups and, unusually, plenty of explicit contract / part-time listings. | Clean single-posting parse. |
42	| `jobs.personio.com` | DACH-heavy, low competition. Real host is `<company>.jobs.personio.com/job/<id>`. | Append `?language=en` — many boards default to German. |
43	| `jobs.lever.co` | Works, but the noisiest. | **Snippets lie about location.** A posting titled "…(Remote, Full-Time)" surfaced under a "remote Europe" query and turned out to be India-only. Also heavy with aggregators (Jobgether) and outsourcing firms. Always fetch before trusting. |
44	
45	Legacy `boards.greenhouse.io/<co>/jobs/<id>` 302-redirects off-host (costs two calls), and
46	`boards.greenhouse.io/embed/job_board` is robots-disallowed. `apply.workable.com` job pages are
47	a client-side SPA that silently degrade to the company's "Current Openings" page — read Workable
48	through its widget API instead (§5).
49	
50	---
51	
52	## 3. Query recipes that returned real hits
53	
54	Role phrase + remote + region, domain-restricted:
55	
56	- `AI automation engineer remote Europe` → n8n, Quora, Quadrivia, Oh (MarTech AI & Automation, remote Europe), Bifrost, DoiT
57	- `"forward deployed engineer" remote Europe` → Cohere, ElevenLabs, Luma, Camunda EMEA
58	- `AI solutions engineer remote EMEA` → Mistral, Camunda, WunderGraph, Omni
59	- `"technical product manager" remote Europe`
60	
61	**Contract intent — put the literal contract vocabulary in the query.** Asking for "contract"
62	generically returns permanent roles; these words work:
63	
64	- `freelance contractor AI automation engineer "contract" remote day rate n8n` → Kairos "Contract Software Engineer", Hippocratic AI "Junior Forward Deployment Engineer (Contract)", a 12-month Ansible AAP contract on join.com, Scalia "AI Automation Specialist (Part time)", G2i
65	- Also try: `"6-month contract"`, `"12-month contract"`, `"fixed-term"`, `(Contract)`, `B2B`, `part time`, `fractional`
66	
67	**Stack keywords are his edge.** `n8n`, `low-code`, `AI agents`, `Bubble.io`, `Playwright`,
68	`Zapier`/`Make`/`Tray.ai` postings are far less crowded than generic "AI Engineer" listings.
69	Run at least one stack-keyword query per sweep.
70	
71	**Company-direct.** For a named company, `WebFetch` its board index —
72	`job-boards.greenhouse.io/<company>` fetches fine as a bulk company-wide listing with no API
73	token — or query `allowed_domains=["jobs.ashbyhq.com"]` with the company name.
74	
75	Unrestricted generic queries (`AI solutions engineer remote EMEA jobs`) return aggregator SEO
76	farms with almost no direct-apply links. Their one use is **host discovery** — that's how
77	`job-boards.eu.greenhouse.io` turned up.
78	
79	---

81	## 4. Job boards worth fetching
82	
83	| Board | What it gives | Verified URL templates |
84	|---|---|---|
85	| **euremotejobs.com** | Best European board tested. Region strings distinguish "Europe" / "EMEA" / worldwide — exactly the filter that matters. Freshest feed seen (listings minutes old). Salary on roughly a third. | `/job-region/remote-jobs-europe/` · `/job-region/remote-jobs-emea/` · `/job-region/{spain,portugal,germany,ireland,uk}/` · `/jobs/remote-software-engineering-jobs/` · `/jobs/remote-data-jobs/` · `/jobs/all-remote-jobs/` |
86	| **remoterocketship.com** | **Signal only** — it surfaces on-target Italy-remote roles other sources miss, but its pages expose no direct-apply URLs, so a row can't be sourced from here. Use it to learn *company + title*, then find the original posting via an ATS search. Keyword + country + recency compose in one URL; EUR salaries, dates to the minute. | `https://www.remoterocketship.com/country/italy?page=1&sort=DateAdded&jobTitle=AI%20Engineer` · `https://www.remoterocketship.com/?page=1&sort=DateAdded&locations=Europe` |
87	| **himalayas.app** | Uniquely states the **region restriction per job** ("Netherlands only", "Global", "United Kingdom only") — kills the biggest time-waster, the secretly-US-only "remote" role. | `/jobs` · `/jobs/countries/italy` · `/jobs/python` · `/jobs/engineering` · `?page=N`. **Serialize these calls** — it 429s under concurrency, and paths don't compose (`/jobs/countries/italy/skills/python` → 404). |
88	| **arbeitnow.com** (JSON) | Clean JSON: title, company, `remote`, `location`, `tags`, `created_at` epoch. DACH-heavy, mixed non-tech — filter hard. | `https://arbeitnow.com/api/job-board-api` |
89	| **remoteok.com** (JSON only) | HTML page is an empty JS shell; the API works. Global overflow. **Its `salary_min`/`salary_max` are `$0` — ignore them.** | `https://remoteok.com/api` |
90	| **aijobs.net** | Best salary transparency of any board (EUR bands on most rows), strongly on-target for AI/ML. Company names don't always extract. | `https://aijobs.net/` — filter params unverified, don't invent them |
91	| **wellfound.com** | US-skewed, no posting dates — but now in scope since he's open to non-EU and contract work. | `https://wellfound.com/role/r/software-engineer` |
92	
93	**Dead or blocked — don't spend calls here:** weworkremotely.com (returns binary),
94	welcometothejungle.com, landing.jobs, jobicy.com, linkedin.com/jobs (all robots-disallowed),
95	nofluffjobs.com (403), EURES / europa.eu jobs portal and jobs.eu (JS shell / bad TLS),
96	workatastartup.com (renders fragments only), remotive.com and workingnomads.com (listing pages
97	render navigation only — no jobs), freelancermap.com (paths 404 without discovery).
98	
99	Freelance marketplaces — Malt, Braintrust, Contra, Upwork, Toptal — are login-walled or
100	client-rendered. Don't burn a sweep on them. Contract work comes through the ATS contract
101	queries in §3, contract-first shops with public boards (e.g. **G2i** on Ashby), and the
102	part-time/contract listings on **join.com** and **euremotejobs.com**.
103	
104	---
105	
106	## 5. Public JSON APIs — use these to verify
107	
108	These fetch as text and expose exactly the fields needed to confirm a posting is live:
109	
110	- **Greenhouse:** `https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/<token>/jobs?content=true` → `absolute_url`, `updated_at`, locations. Best freshness check available.
111	- **Ashby:** `https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/<org>?includeCompensation=true` → `isRemote`, `isListed`, `publishedAt`, `compensation`.
112	- **Lever:** `https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/<co>?mode=json` → `workplaceType` (Remote/Hybrid), location. Fails on very large aggregator boards.
113	- **Workable:** `https://apply.workable.com/api/v1/widget/accounts/<subdomain>?details=true` → the only readable route into Workable.
114	
115	**WebFetch truncates long JSON**, and its summariser will quietly under-report: asking
116	"list all jobs" on a big board returned 7 of N and omitted roles that exist. Ask a *targeted*
117	question instead — "does this board currently list a Forward Deployed Engineer role, and what
118	is its location and posted date?"
119	
120	**A negative answer from a board API is not evidence on its own.** Truncation produces
121	*fabricated* negatives — one read stated four target roles were "not present" when the board
122	simply hadn't been fully returned. Before concluding a role is closed, either get two
123	independent reads that agree, or corroborate with a differently-shaped source. Concluding
124	"closed" wrongly costs him a real opportunity, so the burden of proof sits on the negative.
125	
126	---
127	
128	## 6. Verification traps
129	
130	Search indexes run stale across every ATS, so a posting found in search may already be gone.
131	These are the specific failure modes, and the first one is dangerous because the fetch
132	*succeeds*:
133	
134	1. **Greenhouse closed postings degrade to the board index.** Fetching a dead job URL returns the company's entire open-roles list with the target role absent, and nothing flags it. **Detection rule: if a single-posting fetch comes back describing many different jobs, the posting is closed.** Drop it.
135	2. **Personio closed postings hard-404** even while still indexed in search. Clean failure — just drop.
136	3. **Lever snippets misstate location.** Fetch the posting and read the location from the page body.
137	4. **"Remote" ≠ eligible.** Read the eligibility sentence, not the word "Remote" in the title. Titles like "AI Automation Engineer (Remote – ES/UK only)" are common, and boards sometimes label a region-locked role "worldwide".
138	5. **Aggregators masquerade as employers.** Jobgether, Jobgether-on-Lever, and similar reposts have no named end client. Skip them; find the original posting if the role looks good.
139	6. **Himalayas orders results non-chronologically** — page 1 mixed "2 mins ago" with "27 days ago". Read the date on each row rather than trusting position.
140	7. **Ashby pages return JS shells intermittently.** `meta-title: Jobs` or "You need to enable JavaScript to run this app" means the fetch failed, *not* that the role closed. Go to the org's posting API (§5) — and remember §5's rule that a negative there needs a second read. Three failures like this nearly cost the highest-relevance company of one sweep.
141	
142	---
143	
144	## 7. Freshness
145	
146	- Minute-level ages: euremotejobs, remoterocketship, himalayas, aijobs.net (parse from the page).
147	- Sortable by recency in the URL: only `remoterocketship.com/?sort=DateAdded` is verified.
148	- Programmatic date filtering: only via the JSON APIs (`created_at` / `date` / `epoch` / `updated_at`).
149	- No board tested exposes a verified "posted within N days" parameter — filter client-side.
